reason: The text is dominated by regular human characters with significant agency. Jacob (יַעֲקֹב) is the primary protagonist who actively plans strategy, sends messengers, divides his household and livestock into camps, instructs servants on what to say, negotiates with Esau, and makes decisions about travel and settlement. Esau (עֵשָׂו) is also a regular human character who approaches with 400 men, greets Jacob, and independently decides his own path. Additionally, Jacob's wives (Leah and Rachel), servants (עֲבָדִים), and children all appear as actors performing deliberate actions. These are not passive characters—they make decisions, carry out strategies, and respond to circumstances. While divine elements are present (angels, God's blessing), the narrative fundamentally centers on human characters exercising volition and agency.
